title: A health and social care levy: 1.25% on employers and employees
noun: the health and social care levy
headline: The 2021 levy again: 1.25 points on every NICs rate. About £26bn, static.
description: Reintroduce the Health and Social Care Levy legislated in 2021: 1.25% on employers, employees and the self-employed on the National Insurance base, with the money for health and social care. This card adds up HMRC's figures for a one-point rise in each rate (employer, employee and self-employed, main and additional) and takes 1.25 times the total: the same figures the National Insurance sliders use. In 2021 HM Treasury put the levy together with the dividend tax rise announced beside it at about £12 billion a year; the dividend rise is already in today's baseline, and the employer rate and the earnings it falls on have grown since.

baselinePolicy.text: No levy. Employee NICs 8% and 2%, employer NICs 15% above a frozen secondary threshold; the 2021 levy was repealed before its first separate year.
alreadyIncludes: Employer NICs at 15% with the secondary threshold frozen (Budget 2025, Table 4.1 line 47).

rawSource.note: HMRC's figures for a one-point rise in the employer, employee and self-employed rates, main and additional, added up and multiplied by 1.25: our arithmetic on official figures. The employee rows already include the self-employed (Class 4), so nothing is counted twice.

uprating.head: nics
uprating.note: Shifted to the start year and scaled by the OBR March 2026 forecast for National Insurance receipts, as the National Insurance sliders are (ADR-0004).

caveats: HMRC's figures for a one-point rise in each rate, added up and multiplied by 1.25: our arithmetic on official figures, with HMRC's usual allowance for behaviour and nothing more. HMRC calls larger changes approximate.
The employer share falls on public employers too. If the Treasury tops up public sector budgets for it, as it did in 2022 and 2025, the net yield is lower.

In 2021 HM Treasury put the levy with the dividend tax rise at around £12 billion a year on average over 2022-23 to 2024-25. That dividend rise is already in today's baseline, and the employer rate and the earnings it falls on have grown since.
A higher rate than 1.25% has been reported; the card scores the legislated rate.
The manifesto rules out increasing National Insurance. A levy on the National Insurance base is National Insurance by another name to most readers; whether it counts is contested.

considerations.text: HMRC's rows carry its standard response to a one-point change. A 2.5 point rise in the combined rate on pay is well beyond that: part of the employer share would show up as lower pay and profits over time, and some earnings would move to forms the levy misses.

The manifesto promises not to increase National Insurance. The 2021 levy was a separate tax on the National Insurance base, so reviving it keeps the letter of the promise while testing its spirit. The game marks it amber, not red: the pledge’s words are kept and its spirit is tested, and the benches and the public will say so on Budget day.

interactions.text: Both fall on the same pay: the levy is 1.25 points on the employee side on top of any change here.
Both fall on earnings above the upper limit: the levy is 1.25 points there on top of any change here.
Both fall on the same payroll: the levy is 1.25 points on the employer side on top of any change here.
